narratives.claim: China has India in a 'debt trap' through Belt-and-Road-style lending.
narratives.strongestCase: Chinese state banks did lend heavily to Indian private groups in 2008–2015 (RCom ≈US$3.6bn, Sasan ≈US$1bn, Aircel, Lanco, APML, Essar), took security over licences and plant, and pursued promoters through NCLT and the London Commercial Court; Xi's 2014 visit produced US$2.8bn of bank credit-line pledges and US$1bn+ industrial-park pledges.
narratives.strongestCounter: India is not a BRI participant and has no recorded sovereign bilateral debt to China in World Bank IDS (2010, 2014, 2023); 72% of its bilateral sovereign debt is owed to Japan at 0.1–2.7%. Every Chinese credit in AidData is to a private or SOE borrower at LIBOR-plus commercial spreads, and the largest borrowers defaulted on the Chinese banks, not the reverse — the lenders, not the borrower's sovereign, carried the loss. Debt-trap mechanics (sovereign collateral, asset seizure) are absent.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Discovery of sovereign or sovereign-guaranteed Chinese lending to the Union or a state; or Chinese-bank enforcement seizing strategic Indian infrastructure (none found).

narratives.claim: Japanese ODA loans to India are 'strings-free'.
narratives.strongestCase: Rates of 0.1–2.7% over 30–50 years with 10–15-year grace are far below market; most India loans in the same signing packages are 'General untied'; JICA imposes no policy conditionality of the DPL type; procurement runs through ICB and the executing agency.
narratives.strongestCounter: The largest programme — MAHSR, ¥1.05 trillion — is explicitly 'Tied': JICA's ex-ante evaluation records that both governments 'agreed that the tied loan will be made … in order to utilize the technology and knowledge of Japan', reserving core Shinkansen packages for Japanese suppliers; the training-institute loan is tied too. The string is commercial (supplier exclusivity), not political, and it is disclosed.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: Contract-level data on the Japanese share of MAHSR awards (JICA procurement notices) would size the string; a shift of later tranches to untied terms would weaken it.

narratives.claim: The bullet train is a 'vanity loan' — an expensive prestige project India did not need.
narratives.strongestCase: ¥1,050,000m committed against a 2018 ex-ante cost of ¥1,806,282m, a Dec-2023 planned completion missed while tranche V was still being signed in Dec 2023; tied procurement removes price competition; the yen counterpart and cost escalation could not be verified from Indian sources (NHSRCL unreachable).
narratives.strongestCounter: At 0.1% over 50 years with 15 years' grace, the loan is close to a grant in present-value terms; India bears yen exchange risk but negligible interest; delays trace to Maharashtra land acquisition rather than lender behaviour; JICA's ex-ante document sets out traffic, time-saving and pollution indicators against which the project can be evaluated ex post.
narratives.whatWouldChangeThis: A JICA ex-post evaluation or CAG audit giving realised cost, ridership and the yen-depreciation effect; a Parliament answer on the current ₹ cost and JICA share.

symmetryCheck: The brief's control is Chinese official finance to Indian private companies against Japanese ODA to Indian public projects, on the same fields. Run on both: Japan — sovereign borrower (GoI/DEA), 0.1–2.7% for 30–50 years, 10–15-year grace, disclosed conditions (MAHSR tied; most others untied), named executing agencies, an ex-ante evaluation per loan, zero defaults; China — private/SOE borrowers, LIBOR + 1.8–4.75%, 4–13-year maturities, security over plant and telecom licences, equipment-tied, Sinosure-insured, no public evaluation, three of the four largest borrowers insolvent. The lens that produces an alarming picture of Chinese money (collateral, litigation, promoter guarantees) produces none for Japanese money — but it also produces none for US Ex-Im and DFC, whose Sasan and First Solar loans are equally tied to home-country equipment and equally aimed at competing with China. Read symmetrically, 'tied export finance to Indian private borrowers' is what every ECA does; the discriminating facts about China are the borrowers' quality (the most leveraged groups of the 2008–12 boom) and the outcome (lender losses), not the lending. On the UPA/NDA control: the Chinese private lending peaks under UPA-II (2008–2013) and the JICA MAHSR/metro surge under NDA (2017–2026), but both are lender-and-borrower commercial timing (3G auction 2010, Shinkansen decision 2015), and neither government signed the private loans; no partisan gap survives the date test.
